en: Regarding the "Preface to the Hall of Holy Arrows" (*Seongjeondang seogeok*), which recounts the words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity: I sat in the Hall of Holy Arrows and recounted the words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs from above.

The words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are as vast as mountains and as deep as the accumulation of oceans; why is it that what is recounted here consists of only these few chapters? It is because [I have] specifically selected...
I have recorded here only that which has come within the range of my own vision. Yet, does the scope of my sight end merely with this?
There are many accounts of ordinary events that have not yet been pointed out; there are matters whose principles are profound and subtle, which benefit one’s fundamental nature;
there are those that diagnose the maladies of the Dharma-ending age, striking directly at their very core; and there are those concerning the rigorous practice of the path.
I shall now describe those whose final moments were particularly extraordinary, following this with my own critical assessment; were it otherwise, I would have no leisure to record them.
Furthermore, there are differences between ancient and modern times, as well as precedence among individuals. Why is it that those recorded here appear intermingled and disordered?
It is because I have arranged them according to the nature of their attainments rather than according to chronological order. This is so.
This is the compilation. Although it consists of only some twenty thousand words, the Buddhas' and Patriarchs' earnest efforts on behalf of humanity can be seen at a glance herein.
Each time one unfurls the scroll, it causes the eye of wisdom to become clear and the realization of intelligence to become pure. It is both the sickness and the medicine.
What is correct and what is deviant are each clearly evident, as if pointing at one's own palm.

Only then does one realize that the words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, while appearing to instruct people on the surface, are in fact profound in their transformative power. Two or three like-minded companions, having seen this and appreciated it, each contributed funds to request its carving into woodblocks for circulation.
Do they not, perhaps, grasp my own intention? Therefore, I have briefly composed these few words as a preface to the beginning of the volume, so that—
Those who read this later will be inspired with a surge of enthusiasm and will compose extensive works of their own; thus, it shall not be merely this compilation alone.
Written in the second month of spring in the year of Jihai (1459), by the patched-robed monk Daopai.
Record of the Sangha Hall of Zen Master Hongzhi Jue of Tiantong, composed by Shi Daohui of Gushan, following the ancient accounts of the Holy Arrow Hall.
Now, the smile at Vulture Peak was warm; the sitting at Shaolin was profound.
Cold. From east to west, the lineage was transmitted through thirty-three generations. Old Lu received the robe and bowl and fled; his deeds were manifest and renowned.

Opening and closing, expanding and contracting, with waves and flames of brilliance, he spoke from the mouth at will and responded from the heart as it moved. The Way was transmitted and the vessel received it.
When the source is deep, the stream is long. At Mount Nanyue and Qingyuan, successive generations have produced worthy men. Some have held a silent lineage, withdrawing into obscurity and seclusion;

they effaced their traces from the world to investigate the mysteries of life and death. Eating pine needles and wearing lotus leaves, nesting in trees or sitting upon grass mats, they remained hidden and did not seek fame, nurturing themselves until they reached maturity.
Those who admired their style would follow them as teachers and friends, tilling the soil, planting crops, husking grain, gathering water, and preparing food for them.

He boiled the wild herbs from the streams and marshes, content with his own meager sustenance. As those who had traveled far from home gathered in increasing numbers, he established a Sangha hall and presided over them.

There, the assembly of teachers and friends worked together; they stripped away emotional attachments and severed intellectual cleverness, casting aside conventional learning and discarding the status of a master, until the wondrous essence of the mind’s emptiness was fully realized.

The essence of the school is a living eye, which manifests in its practical applications; thus, its capabilities are fully realized. At the end of the Jianyan era, people suffered from the chaos of war and separation.
Across Xianghan and Jianghuai, armies and fires ravaged and plundered everything. Monasteries of venerable elders were mostly reduced to overgrown ruins.

Wearing robes of coarse wool and carrying their staffs and alms bowls, [the Master] sought refuge at the Chan seat of Siming in the southeast—a place long renowned as the "Little Mount Lu"—located six *li* east of the prefectural city.
Ten *li* away lies the Tiantong Monastery. The mountain winds and turns with an air of profound seclusion; the pines grow stooped and their bark is wrinkled.
Verdant walls cling to creeping vines, glistening with moisture as the mist dries; a solitary rainbow rests across the ravine, its clarity enhanced as it washes away the dust.

During my four years of residence on this mountain, disciples from the ten directions have flocked here like clouds and water, such that the buildings could no longer contain them. Now, the Bhikṣu Xingshen has suddenly arrived.
The petitioner said: "In the cypress courtyard there is a son who sits in the open air and sleeps beneath the eaves; he has not even a single foot or cubit of space to receive his single alms-bowl.
I wish to solicit from the pure faithful to enlarge his hall. May this be granted? I nodded my head in agreement. Subsequently, craftsmen entered the forest and axes resounded through the valley.

After more than a year, the foundation stones were laid out and the columns stood in rows; the beams spanned across and the rafters clustered together. The ridge-poles spread like wings, and the roof tiles were arranged like fish scales.
The roofed structure consists of fourteen bays front-to-back and twenty frames. It features three corridors and two courtyards; the ground floor has no enclosing walls.

It measures two hundred chi in length and sixteen *zhang* in width. The windows, casements, beds, and couches are profoundly bright and strictly clean. Ten thousand people may eat and rest here with spacious ease and leisure.
Planning began in the winter of the *Renzi* year of the Shaoxing era, and the construction was completed in the spring of the *Jiayin* year. In total—
It cost fifteen thousand taels of gold and more. It is warm in winter and cool in summer; incense burns by day and lamps shine by night. One opens the alms bowl for a meal and sits with feet washed.

Amidst these surroundings, one may plow and herd cattle, while being guided toward tranquility. In autumn, it reflects the depths of an ancient well; in spring, it enters the mechanism of transformation.
Profound and silent, it achieves its perfection; brilliant and radiant, it employs its light. Water flows when its basins are full; a valley echoes as it follows a call.
When principle accords with equality, wisdom responds spontaneously. Whether in motion or stillness, dignified demeanor provides mutual benefit like acupuncture and moxibustion.

One examines and restrains outflows, polishes away scars, sharpens the luster, and grinds away jagged edges. Thus, one sets a lofty standard to reach afar, emulating the footsteps of the ancients, and seeking the Way through the mind.

Exerting effort and the like, yet failing to fulfill their intent; with inferior spirit and corrupt learning, they long for ease and desire speed. They take mechanical artifice as their path and dissipation as their track.
They plow at empty words and go hungry without any harvest; they wage war with forceful sophistry, yet achieve victory that leads nowhere.
What one sees, hears, and habitually practices clouds one’s understanding and deluges the mind; this is what the Buddhas and Patriarchs condemn and where demons and heretics find their opportunity.

When such afflictions and sprouts of corruption begin to emerge, they must not be allowed to run wild. One must ascend the heights of Mount Kunlun and dam the waters of the Yangtze and Yellow Rivers to wash away the filth from one’s liver and gallbladder, and to clear the cataracts from the eyes of the heart and mind.
Thus, the traces of birth and extinction vanish while the wondrous remains; the tracks of existence and non-existence are obliterated.
The excessive [delusions] have been surpassed; the dream of the great night has been shattered; doubts spanning eternal kalpas have been uprooted; the aspiration for renunciation has been fulfilled;
and the purpose of traveling as a pilgrim has been accomplished. My companions who followed me are now nearly equal to this attainment.
The critique states: Tiantong’s Way was lofty and his cultivation pure; his learning was vast and his knowledge comprehensive. One may gain a general insight into this from this record. He said:

"To hollow out emotion and excise intellect, to cast aside study and dismiss the teacher—thus the subtle reaches its ultimate and the mind becomes empty. The lineage is thorough and the eye is alive. He also said:
"Plowing and herding within that space, awakening and guiding through stillness. Autumn reflects in the ancient well; spring enters the mechanism of transformation. How profound!"
Silent accomplishment is radiant and brilliant. It is further said that through the postures of movement and stillness, one benefits from mutual correction like acupuncture and moxibustion;

by examining and restraining leaks, one polishes away scars and sharpens the luster of the mind. By grinding away the protruding edges, one reaches lofty heights and far-reaching goals, following in the footsteps of the ancients.
Alas! If students dwelling in the Sangha hall can truly take this as their standard for advancing on the Path, what more could be desired?
I lament that great matters are not discerned; perhaps they conceal what they ought to treat as an ailment and violate what requires their remedy.
I know them only as those who are self-destructive and self-abandoning. Therefore, I have recorded these writings, for they seem to belong to those with true resolve.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: At that time, the Tathāgata, surrounded by the fourfold assembly, praised and expounded the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

Having entrusted it to Ānanda (Pītimat), commanding him to receive and uphold it, he manifested supernatural powers before the great assembly, causing everyone to see the land of the Buddha Akṣobhya (Sanskrit:
Akṣobhya). They beheld that Tathāgata, surrounded before and behind by śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, proclaiming the Dharma for the vast multitude.

He preached the sublime Dharma and manifested the marks of that land’s majestic purity. Then, the Buddha withdrew his supernormal power, and in an instant, he caused this assembly to no longer see it.
At that time, the Buddha asked Ānanda, "Ānanda, do you still see the land and the assembly of Akṣobhya Tathāgata?
Ānanda replied, "I no longer see those things; they are no longer within the range of these eyes."
Therefore, the Buddha told Ānanda: "You should know that all phenomena are likewise so. They are not the objective domain traversed by the eye-faculty and the other faculties.
A phenomenon does not traverse a phenomenon; a phenomenon does not see a phenomenon; a phenomenon does not know a phenomenon; a phenomenon does not realize a phenomenon.
Ānanda, you should know that in the nature of all phenomena, there is nothing that can see, nothing that can traverse, nothing that can know, and nothing that can realize."
...is without movement and without activity. Why is this? Because all phenomena are like empty space;
they possess no functional activity, for their nature is utterly remote from both the grasper and the grasped. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"You should know that the previously cultivated notions of impermanence and suffering are not ultimate reality. For example, it is like people in the springtime who, at a great bathing place..."
In a pond, they were playing by boat when a lapis lazuli gem was lost, sinking into the deep water.
At that time, all the people entered the water together to search for the gem, competing to seize tiles, stones, grass, wood, sand, and gravel.
Each person thought they had found the lapis lazuli bead and joyfully brought it out, only to realize it was not the real one. At that moment, the true gem remained as before within the water.

The commentary states: Formerly, when the Patriarch Daoming commanded his disciples to each speak of their realization, the nun Zongchi said, "As I see it, it is like the Elder Ānanda seeing the land of Akṣobhya Buddha;
once seen, it is never seen again. The Patriarch said, "You have attained my flesh.
Chan Master Zhiche presented a verse to the Sixth Patriarch which said: "Because of guarding the impermanent mind, the Buddha expounds the permanent dharma..."
Regarding the nature of permanence: those who do not understand skillful means are like those who gather pebbles from a spring pond.
I have cited two such instances and asked my fellow students from what scriptural sources they derive; often they are unable to answer, and some even resort to mere conjecture.

Later, upon reading the *Prajñāpāramitā* and *Nirvāṇa* sūtras, I finally saw them there. Only then did I realize that the words of the ancients were never uttered lightly, whereas later generations...
Scholars today have both heard and seen little, and are often reckless in their judgments; therefore, I have recorded this together [with the following].
The Master of Xingkong Hermitage was a native of Hanzhou. Having long relied upon Sīxīn (Sicong) and attained realization, he traveled to Xiushui to follow the legacy of Chuangzhi (Chuanzi).
He built a thatched hut in the wilds of Qīnglóng and amused himself by blowing an iron flute, composing many verses. Those who obtained them...

"Be sure to treasure this. Regarding dwelling in the mountains, he said: 'When both mind and dharmas are forgotten, one is still separated by delusion; when form and emptiness are non-dual, a trace of dust remains.
The hundred birds do not come and spring passes once more; who knows who is the person dwelling in the hermitage?

Furthermore, he warned the assembly: 'Studying the Way is like guarding a forbidden city: by day, guard against the six thieves; by night, remain alert. If the commander-in-chief of the central army can carry out his orders, [the city is secure].'"
"Without moving a blade of grass, one governs a time of great peace. It is also said: "Eating without plowing and wearing clothes without sericulture;

pure and leisurely beyond the mundane world, one finds fulfillment in this sagely age. Yet, if you have not yet penetrated the pivot of the Patriarch’s gate, you must at least maintain your intent and seek the advantage.
It is further said: "At all twelve hours of the day, do not let your work cease. Examine, examine until it reaches the infinite. You must penetrate thoroughly to the very bottom of that infinity."
He leveled the first peak of Mount Sumeru. During the Jianyan era, when Xu Ming rebelled, he passed through Wuzhen and carried out a massacre;
many of the people fled, but the Master alone went forth carrying his staff. When the rebels saw his imposing and extraordinary appearance, they suspected he must be a hidden conspirator.
When asked why he had come, the Master said, "I am a Chan practitioner; I wish to reach Mijin Temple. The bandits were enraged and intended to behead him.
The Master said, "If you want my head, then cut it off. Why be angry? My death is certain; I only wish to have one meal as a final send-off. The bandits served him meat and rice.
After the Master finished his regular midday meal and performed the ritual for the deceased, he said, "Who can compose a text for me to offer as a sacrifice?"
The bandit smiled but did not answer. The Master asked for a brush and wrote in large characters: "Alas! O Spirit!

That it has toiled me with life is the fault of the Great Mass (the Earth). That it has employed me with longevity is the error of Yin and Yang. That it has deprived me of wealth is because the Five Elements were not in harmony.
That it has constrained me with my fate is because the timing of the day was not auspicious. Alas! How profound! Fortunately, there is that which transcends the dust [of the mundane world]..."
The Way: to awaken to one’s own nature and accord with that wondrous mind. Then, as for this wondrous mind, with whom could it not be in harmony?
Above, it accords with the true transformation of all Buddhas; below, it merges with the ignorance of ordinary beings. Not a speck of dust stirs; it is fundamentally and spontaneously perfected.
How wondrous! How wondrous! The sun and moon are not sufficient to be called luminous; heaven and earth are not sufficient to be called great. It is vast and majestic.
Magnificent and towering! Unhindered and unobstructed. For over sixty years, he blended his light with the mundane world; for forty-two years since ordination, he has wandered at ease and in freedom.
He rejoices upon meeting people, yet does not bow even before a Buddha. How joyful! How joyful! What a pity for this young man—his refined elegance was so radiant.
He returns home with composure, entrusting himself to the spring breeze; his body is like empty space, ultimately never...
"Destroyed! May you enjoy this! He then raised his chopsticks and ate heartily. The bandits laughed loudly. When he had finished eating, he spoke again:

"Since we have encountered these calamitous times of rebellion and chaos, I am a man of great joy and vigor. Now is precisely the right moment to seize the opportunity; I request that you cut me in two with a single stroke."
He then shouted loudly, "Chop! Chop! The rebels were struck with awe and alarm; they prostrated themselves to apologize for their transgression and ordered guards to escort him out.

Thus, the Lu she temple in Wuzhen was spared from burning, which was truly due to the Master's grace. When both the clergy and the laity heard of this, their reverence for him increased all the more. This was in the winter of the Gengshen year of the Xiangxing era.
He performed a great service by boring a hole and blocking it. He wrote a letter to Chan Master Shi of Xuedou, saying: "I shall be buried in water.
In the year of Renxu, Shi arrived and saw that [the body] was still there; he composed a verse to mock him, saying: "Alas, old Xingkong!"
"I was just about to feed the fish and turtles. I did not leave with a settled mind; I merely went about telling people [of my intent].

The Master read the verse and said with a smile, "I shall wait for my elder brother to come and provide witness. He then ordered that this be announced throughout the fourfold assembly. When the assembly had gathered, the Master preached the essentials of the Dharma and further spoke a verse:
"To die while sitting or standing is not as good as a water burial. First, it saves the need for firewood; second, it saves the digging of a grave. Letting go of the hand..."
He then departed. How refreshing! Who is the one who understands? The Boatman Monk—his lofty style is difficult to emulate after a thousand years;
his single song of the fisherman is rarely sung by others. He then sat cross-legged in the basin and went downstream with the tide.

The assembly followed him all the way to the seashore, their eyes nearly failing them from gazing so far. The Master took up a scoop to bail out the water and returned; the crowd pressed forward to watch, but there was no water left.
He entered [the water] again, riding the current away, and cried out: "The boatman of old returned to his hometown; where his traces vanished, his wondrousness is immeasurable.
His true wind is sent everywhere to those who know it; he plays his iron flute crosswise to conclude the performance.

As the sound of the flute wailed and choked, amidst the vast expanse, they saw him cast the flute into the air and submerge. The multitude mourned him with longing, depicting his image and honoring him.
Three days later, he sat cross-legged upon the sand as if alive. Monastics and laypeople vied with one another to go and welcome him back home. He remained for five days, after which he was cremated.
The śarīras, as large as soybeans, were beyond counting. Two cranes circled in the air and only departed once the fire had been extinguished.
The assembly enshrined the śarīras and sacred bones and erected a stupa at Qinglong.

The commentary says: Alas! Life and death are indeed momentous matters, yet [this master] acted with such ease and mastery amidst the edge of a sword and the surging tide, attaining a state of transcendent self-realization.
Had he not clearly realized the fundamental roots of the Way and thoroughly practiced its path, how could this have been possible?
How could one possibly attain this? When those in the world who practice the "mercury-silver" Chan encounter fire, they immediately melt away, losing what they were meant to preserve;
seeing this, one can perhaps receive a slight warning.
The Record of the Painted Waves Studio by Chan Master Hong Juefan. In the summer of the first year of the Jianzhong Jinggu era, I was a guest at Dongshan.
In the eastern chamber of the Chan-yue Hall, there were no superfluous belongings; there stood only a single bed covered with a coarse mat. Several volumes of books were propped against my pillow.
Facing south, I opened a window to take in the splendors of the surrounding mountains. When my eyes grew weary, I would cast aside the books and sit.
Lying down, I contemplate the connection of the mountains; their forms are inexhaustible, and my joy in them likewise knows no satiety.
During the great heat of the three summer months, even the couches where I sit are warm. The shade of the forest, though it brushes against me, is insufficient to dispel the fearsome sun.
There was a man from Shu who had mastered the "living water" legacy of Sun Zhimi; he painted for me upon the wall a scene of crashing waves and vast expanses of mist to bring in the cool air.
He cast off his robes and sat in a relaxed posture; with a single stroke of his brush, he brought it to completion. I was struck with wonder and sighed in admiration, saying: "How extraordinary!

Within the space of a single wall and in the brief span of a moment, you have captured the vast landscape of the Yangtze and Lake Dongting. With its majestic waves and raging eddies, its hollows and elevations in a thousand forms, there is an inexhaustible variety of change.
As a dark wind slowly approaches, one’s hair stands on end and one’s bones tremble; suddenly, it is as if one were upon a boat on Lake Dongting."
I gazed at the frosty dawn. Could there be anything more perilous, awe-inspiring, or swift than this? The practitioner raised his staff and pointed toward it, saying to me:
"A dragon-drawn vessel of ten thousand *hu* capacity proceeds with slow, winding grace; it seems as if it wishes to cross, yet it acts with cautious reverence.

It is like a high minister of state, entrusted with great responsibility and heavy duty, contemplating how to save the people and repay the nation. The prows and sterns of the ships are joined together."
Their tails lashing, they chase one another up and down; now moving, now lingering, like the bustling crowds on a career path who advance yet find no end.
Fish and dragons undergo transformations, appearing and disappearing in turn, like those who suddenly rise from obscurity to noble status, only to be suddenly cast aside.
A single-leafed boat defies the headwinds and dances amidst the surging waves, transcendent and self-satisfied, as if—
His moral character was extraordinary and transcendent; he mingled with the common people without distinction. The swift and perilous waves of the world—there must be something akin to this.

Therefore, I have depicted him. As for the white gulls and shorebirds, drifting aimlessly with the current as if they were unattached, they are like those of our own kind who dwell among green mountains and keep company with white clouds; yet even they still long to soar high and travel far.

I drew [the brush] but could not follow it as it surged forward. Feeling my way over the places where the waves rose and surged, and observing the density and fineness between the strokes, I said to him:
"Is there truly such a thing as arising and ceasing, or change and transformation? He replied: "There is none.

Indeed, the flourishing and decline of heaven and earth and the myriad things, the coming and going of cold and heat throughout antiquity and today, and the cycles of right and wrong, honor and disgrace, pursue one another...
It is inexhaustible. Yet birth, death, sorrow, and affliction pursue one without respite;
they are interwoven and disordered like a honeycomb, like tangled silk, or like waves painted upon a surface—yet from the very beginning, there has never been any arising or ceasing, nor any change.
That people are deluded and falsely alarm themselves at this is like a child who draws a picture and then fears it himself. Thus it was with the great ones of antiquity...
The Sages are all able to sport freely within this; thus it is said: "This Dharma abides in its own place; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant.
It is also said: "All dharmas are eternally quiescent; they possess no marks of arising or ceasing.

Even the elders of the land of the *qū-ér* (horses and colts) in Zhendan say: "It is like drawing patterns upon water—neither born nor extinguished. How could you suddenly forget this? At that time...
This man of the Way looked at me and smiled, saying, "I wish to follow you in your travels. Consequently, he named his study "Painted Waves" (*Huālàng*) and wrote a record for it.
My critique says:
In years past, I read东坡’s (Dongpo’s) "Rhapsody on the Red Cliff" (*Chìhè fù*). I already admired the ingenuity and subtlety of its prose, and I also admired...
The profundity and subtlety of its principles are such that it is said there is none in the world who surpasses it.

Later, upon reading this record by Juefan, which uses surging waves as metaphors for preaching the Dharma and exhaustively reveals the innermost depths of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, I find its prose so expansive, vast, and magnificent that I cannot fathom how many "Red Cliffs" he must have already swallowed and spat out from within his breast. How could this be the work of a mere literary man or scholar?

How could this be something he was capable of achieving? The Master once said of himself: "In my youth, I was orphaned. I knew that reading books was a pleasure, yet I could not grasp its essential points.
When I took up the brush, it felt as if someone were pulling at my elbow; it was like a mute wishing to speak, but with his intent stifled.
My tongue was large and thick, and I laughed frequently. However, at the age of sixteen or seventeen, I followed Dongsan Yun."

At the hermitage, he studied the supramundane Dharma and suddenly attained self-confidence free from doubt. He could recite seven thousand characters of the classics upon hearing them once, and his pen flowed with a thousand words;
progress of this magnitude can be expected at every step. Alas! The benefit that the study of the Way brings to a person need not be discussed merely in terms of the moment of death and rebirth;
that it benefits one’s literary expression in such a way is itself sufficient cause for self-confidence. Now, observe this record.
This is indeed so. Hongzhi Jue resided at Tiantong, while Dahui Zonggao resided at Yuyuang; the two were separated by some twenty *li*.
They exchanged the joy of the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*) through constant correspondence, their visits never ceasing. One day, Hongzhi went to the home of Wei Sicheng Jinke, where there was a hall.

It is called the "Six Profound Stillnesses" (*ṣaḍ-prasāda*), which derives its meaning from the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra*’s principle that the cessation of the six sense-bases is uniformly profound stillness. I request a verse to elucidate this intent.
Zhiyi inscribed it as follows: "When wind and waves have not arisen, one beholds the spiritual source; When the six bases have vanished, the body returns to profound stillness."
Only when all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature can one sit; in the space of a single snap of the fingers, the gate is suddenly opened.

The cold plum blossoms by the hedge herald an early spring; the wild snow before the lattice window does not darken the night. The myriad phenomena, as vast as the universe, are sealed by the mind-seal;

all sensory dusts are transcended and cleared, wondrously leaving no trace. Shortly thereafter, Dahui arrived in succession and requested a verse in response. Dahui then composed this verse, saying: "Neither profound stillness..."
Stir this fountain of the Dharma; when the opportunity arises, do not disdain the provisional names that remain. Only a man of extraordinary spirit can enter the boundless and vast gateway.
Myriad phenomena interlace yet are fundamentally non-dual; the six windows are never obscured by day or night.
Reflecting back on the affairs of the Elder Pang, there is no difference: casting a sword into the void—how could there be any trace?
The critique states: Some may doubt that the two masters' paths were identical, given that their words seem to suggest a distinction between sudden and gradual enlightenment. Why is this?

It is simply because, when following the theme to develop their insights, Hongzhi set a magnificent standard at the outset; then, exerting his full strength in a spirited display, Dahui claimed the prize at the conclusion.
Furthermore, when Hongzhi preached the Dharma for the Temple Administrator, he could not avoid being preoccupied with every step;
whereas Dahui spoke directly of the dharma-gate practiced within his own mind, which was thus vast, expansive, and boundless.
Chan Master Yuangui of Mount Song resided at Pangwu on the mountain. One day, a strange man arrived, wearing a tall cap and trousers with leggings, accompanied by a great many followers.
He moved with light steps and composed ease, and came to pay his respects to the Great Master.

Upon seeing that the man’s appearance was extraordinary and magnificent beyond the ordinary, the Master addressed him, saying, "Welcome, O benevolent one! For what purpose have you come? The man replied, "Do you not recognize me, Master?"
“I am indeed. The Master said, “I regard Buddhas and sentient beings as equal; I view them all with a single eye. How could I make such distinctions?
The spirit said, “I am this mountain deity, capable of bringing life and death upon people. How can you, Master, look upon me with but a single eye? The Master replied:
I am fundamentally unborn; how could you cause me to die? I regard my body as equal to space, and I regard myself as equal to you.
Can you destroy space or yourself? If you could indeed destroy space and yourself, then I would be neither born nor extinguished.
Since you cannot even do this, how much less can you cause me to be born or to die? The Spirit bowed his head and said, "I too am clever."
"O Honorable One, how could I have known that you, a teacher, possessed such vast wisdom and eloquence? I pray that you grant me the true precepts so that I may cross over the world.
The Teacher said, "Since you have requested the precepts, you already possess them. Why is this? Because there is no precept apart from the precept itself;
what further precept could there be? The deity said, "This principle is obscure to me as I hear it. I merely sought the precepts from my teacher."
As a disciple, [the master] prepared a seat for him, took up the incense burner, and set out the ritual table, saying: "I shall confer upon you the five precepts.
If you can uphold them, you should say 'I can'; if you cannot, you should say 'no. Say: 'I respectfully receive the instruction. The master asked: "Can you refrain from sexual misconduct?
[The disciple] replied: "I am also married. The master said: "That is not what I mean. I mean that you must have no lustful desire. [The disciple] replied: "Yes."

[The disciple] replied, "I can. The Master said, "Can you refrain from stealing? He replied, "What lack have I that I would steal? How could I take anything by theft? The Master said, "That is not what I mean.

I mean that you might enjoy blessings for the licentious and bring calamity upon the virtuous for failing to make offerings. [The disciple] said, "I can. The Master said, "Can you refrain from killing?
He replied, "I truly hold the handle of authority; how could I say I do not kill? The Master said, "That is not what I mean. I mean that there is..."
"Excessive error is confusion and doubt. [The student] said, "I can. The Master said, "Can you avoid being deluded?

[The student] said, "I am upright; how could I be deluded? The Master said, "I do not mean this. I mean that your actions before and after do not accord with the Will of Heaven. [The student] said, "I can. The Master said:
"Have you not been ruined by wine? He replied, "I have. The Master said, "The above is what constitutes the Buddha's precepts.
He further said, "Uphold them with a conscious mind, yet do not cling to them with a constrained mind; act for the sake of others with a conscious mind, yet do not harbor thoughts of your own body.

[The Memorial] Your servant offers his humble thanks. Your servant reflects upon himself: by nature his station was humble and lowly, born from amidst the weeds.

Since childhood, he has ardently admired the Gate of Emptiness (*śūnyatā*). With pure sincerity, he vowed to eliminate all external entanglements; with keen resolve, he sought only to explore the Inner Scriptures.

At times, he forgot to eat while attending to inquiries, or stood in the snow to seek knowledge. For seventeen years, he endured the hardships of wind and frost, traveling between the north and south across several [provinces].

Beyond a thousand *li*, he finally beheld the heart-monkey cease its leaping and the mind-horse halt its gallop. His body took refuge in the clouds of Shao-shi, and his head turned as white as the snow of Chu-shan.

As he attained honor and reached the heights of fortune, repeatedly basking in the waves of imperial grace, he investigated the Way and discoursed on emptiness, vowing to repay the virtue of Heaven and Earth.
He opened the ignorant and released the obstructed, sending forth disciples like clouds and water racing across the stars, so that they might propagate the benefit [of the Dharma].

This is entirely due to the grace of Your Majesty’s sagely wisdom. Furthermore, having repeatedly received the imperial summons of the phoenix decree and frequently attended the dragon court, I have successively been granted proclamations and bestowed with layered honors and gifts.

Reflecting upon myself, I am filled with melancholy; how could I repay such kindness even at the cost of my life? Yet, I did not expect that this humble steed of mine would now be so advanced in years.

Do not seek awakening within delusion. Let the morning sun rise and set as many times as it will. Within the body of form lies the formless body; upon the path of ignorance lies the path of non-arising.

Are you not deluded by the roots and dust of birth and death? Furthermore, as you engage in the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—do you maintain this awareness?
Receiving with reverence and responding with solemnity, when putting on clothes, eating, and performing various tasks, can you discern each and every one as being truly real?

When hearing it said that there is a Buddha or no Buddha, that there are sentient beings or no sentient beings, or hearing praise or blame, or what is right or wrong, can you maintain a single mind without wavering?
Furthermore, upon hearing of the wisdom of differentiation, can you clearly and thoroughly understand both its nature and its characteristics?

He is proficient in both principle and phenomena; he is unimpeded in either. There is not a single dharma whose source he does not discern. Even when a thousand sages appear in the world, can there be any doubt?

Thoroughly penetrate the source of the patriarchs’ own nature until you reach the stage of non-learning and freedom from doubt. Only at this time may you cease formal study, extinguish the wandering mind, and rest in ashes.
Whether acting for yourself, then meditative contemplation will accord with reality; or acting for others, then you may provide skillful means and instruction. Even if you cannot do so...

How difficult! How could it be in vain? The Third Patriarch said: "A difference of a hair’s breadth results in worlds as far apart as heaven and earth.

Chan Master Yuanwu presented this recorded discourse on the Dharma. A brilliant and noble monk, possessing outstanding insight and extraordinary character, resolutely cast off his cap;
he regarded worldly status, reputation, and fame as mere drifting dust, floating clouds, and echoes in a valley.

With the great root-capacity of former lives, he knew this segment [of the Way] which transcends birth and death, surpasses the sages and the mundane, and is that which the Tathāgatas of the three periods have realized.
The adamantine true essence has been the wondrous mind transmitted solely through the successive patriarchs.
With every step they take, they trample like fragrant elephants and soar like golden-winged garuḍas, seeking to gallop and fly above the myriad classes of beings by the hundreds of millions.

Cutting through the stream and brushing the heavens, how could they deign to be like geese, cranes, swallows, or sparrows, confined to petty victories and defeats at high and low levels, or to the flicker of lightning and sparks from flint? In that instant—*pīep*.
Does this not turn profit into harm? Therefore, the great sages of antiquity did not record trivial matters nor scheme for shallow, mundane ends.

They resolved their wills upon transcending the Buddhas and Patriarchs, shouldering the heavy responsibility that all others are unable to bear, universally ferrying across the four modes of birth and nine classes of beings, uprooting suffering to grant peace, shattering the ignorance that obstructs the Way, and breaking the poisonous madness of nescience.
The arrow. Plucking it out, the Dharma-eye sees the thorn; the natural radiance of one's own ground becomes clear and serene, and the countenance prior to the empty kalpa becomes manifest.
With all one’s heart and every effort, undaunted by cold or heat, abandoning sleep and forgetting food, one applies oneself with intent to cultivate conduct.
Purifying the three karmas, beneath the three wooden rafters, one causes the monkey of the mind to die and the horse of the will to be slain, until one is as still as a withered tree.
Resembling a rotten stump or a stubborn stone, one suddenly pierces through them; how could this be obtained from another? One uncovers a great hidden treasury.

Yet, like a bright torch in a dark room, one stations a warship at the strategic pass to realize great liberation. Without giving rise to a single thought, one instantaneously achieves perfect enlightenment.

he exerts the four unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), establishing a single pivot and hanging a single phrase, manifesting a single supreme sign.

Thus, he causes all sentient beings—whether mundane or sagely, animate or inanimate—to alike look up to his majestic radiance and equally receive its protective shade. Yet, even this is not yet the point where all merit and achievement are transcended. Turning the head once more, he stands amidst the thousand sages.
It cannot be confined. All spirits look up to it with no door of entry; the various heavens have no path to offer flowers. How could demons or heretics dare to peer at it from the side?
Cast away views and knowledge; shed off the mysterious and the subtle; cast aside all deliberate activity; there is only eating when hungry and drinking when thirsty.
At first, one does not even know what it means to have a mind or to be without a mind, nor what it means to possess mindfulness or lose mindfulness;

how much less could one harbor further attachment to former intellectual understandings, profound phrases and marvelous words, the analytical divisions of the nature of reality, the shackles of names and forms, or even the "Buddha-view" and "Dharma-view" that shake the earth and overturn the heavens?

Those who are eloquent and sharp-witted according to worldly convention merely entangle and bind themselves; they are like those who enter the sea to count its sands—what reliance can there be in such things?

Being equal as great men, you should attend to your duties, confront challenges, and stand out among the crowd. To fulfill your own original vows is itself the fundamental state of great mind, great vision, and great liberation;
it is to be a true person of the Way, free from conditioned activity and mundane affairs.

The evaluation states: This record of teachings has not yet been included among the Dharma heirs of the Buddha-fruit; he may have been a member of another lineage or a scholar who was invited to participate in the Dharma assembly.

thus, the Dharma discourses he presented are as vast and profound as these. Indeed, this is what is meant by "teaching according to the capacity of the recipient. It was not [merely for the sake of fame].
This is superficial. Furthermore, this chapter serves as a path for entering the Way, its beginning and end perfectly complete, in profound accord with the Five Ranks (Wuwei) teaching of Dongshan.

Chan Master Da Hong’en was a close friend of the layman Wujin (Inexhaustible), Zhang Gong Shangying. Wujin once sent a letter inquiring about the essential tenets of the Three Teachings, stating:

"In the third fascicle of the *Cheng weishi lun shu* (Commentary on the Demonstration of Consciousness-Only), it is said that the heterodox views of the Western Regions do not exceed four types of views.

The Confucianism and Daoism of this land likewise do not exceed these four views. For instance, Zhuangzi and Laozi reckon 'spontaneity' (*ziran*) as the cause. [The text continues: "It is capable of..."

That which gives birth to the myriad things is a false cause. The *I Ching* says, "The Supreme Ultimate gives birth to the Two Polarities. To take the Supreme Ultimate as the cause is likewise a false cause.
If one claims that "the alternation of Yin and Yang is called the Way" and that it can give birth to the myriad things, this too is a false cause.

If one calculates that the One is non-being (*śūnyatā*), then this is to be without a cause. Now I wonder: is the "self-so-ness" (*svabhāva*) of Laozi the same as the external paths of the Western heavens?
They are naturally different. Why is this so? Laozi said: "Always be without desire, and thereby observe its subtlety; always have desire, and thereby observe its boundaries.
To be without desire is to be constant; to have boundaries is already to have entered the Way. To call this a "perverse cause"—how could there be any reason for such a claim?
The *Yi* says: "One yin and one yang—this is called the Way. Yin and yang being unfathomable—this is called the Mysterious."

"Spirit. As for this "Spirit," it is a term used to describe that which wondrously permeates all things. It is quiescent and motionless, yet when stimulated, it immediately penetrates the affairs of the world.
Now, you instead treat the Way of Yin and Yang and transformation as a false cause, and cast aside the unfathomable Spirit.

"How could there not be an explanation? I hope you will provide instructions following this letter so that I may sever the net of doubt. The Master replied: "The schools of the non-Buddhist outsiders in the Western Regions have many paths;
yet, when their essential convergence is examined, they do not go beyond the four views of existence and non-existence. These are called the view of existence..."

There is the view of non-existence, the view of both existence and non-existence, and the view of neither existence nor non-existence. Indeed, if one does not take this very mind to be the Way, then the Way is not possessed by oneself;
therefore, it is called an external path (tīrthika). If one does not take all phenomena to be the mind, then phenomena will vary according to one's views.

Therefore, it is called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). For instance, if one says "it exists," then existence implies non-existence; if one says "it does not exist," then non-existence implies the absence of existence.

When there is both existence and non-existence, views of existence arise in competition; when there is neither existence nor non-existence, views of non-existence arise. This also applies to the view that it both exists and does not exist.
The view of neither existence nor non-existence is likewise so. Indeed, if one cannot free oneself from various views, there is no means to clarify one’s own mind;

and if there is no means to clarify one’s own mind, one cannot know the Right Path. Therefore, a sutra says: "Regarding the teachings expressed through words and phrases, those of small intelligence falsely discriminate.
Unable to comprehend their own minds, how can they know the Right Path? It further says: "The view of existence..."
This is precisely defilement; this is not yet seeing. To be far removed from all views—only in this way does one see the Buddha.

Judging by this, the heterodox and the orthodox follow different paths, precisely because their realizations through view differ. Thus, Liangjie [Qingliang] [cites that] according to the reckonings of Zhuangzi and Laozi, the Way (*Dao*) and its phenomena are spontaneous (*ziran*), capable of generating the myriad things;
the *Yijing* says that the Great Ultimate (*Taiji*) generates the two polarities, the alternating Yin and Yang.

This is what is called the Way (*dharma*). To take *ziran* (spontaneity) and the Great Ultimate (*taiji*) as the cause, and to claim that the alternation of Yin and Yang constitutes the Way capable of generating the myriad things, is a calculation based on a false cause.
To claim that "One" is emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is to posit no cause at all. Let us examine this through discussion: Now, the three realms are but mind;
the myriad conditions are of one principle. Because the mind arises, phenomena arise; because the mind ceases, phenomena cease. Extending this reasoning broadly:

It encompasses all phenomena (*sarvabhāva*) yet is not a unifying entity that governs them; it reaches ultimate quiescence (*nirvāṇa*) yet is not non-existence. It is neither non-existence nor not non-existence;

it is neither existence nor not existence. Once these four attachments have vanished and these hundred negations have been dispelled, then "natural causality" becomes mere conceptual play (*prapañca*), and both "emptiness" and "reality" are equally provisional designations (*prajñapti*). As for what is called the "Great... [it is likewise so].
The ultimate of Yin and Yang can give birth to the myriad things; being both eternally non-existent and eternally existent, this constitutes the gateway to all wonders.

That Yin and Yang cannot be fathomed is what we call the boundless spirit. Although the sages established their teachings and demonstrated various methods for awakening, since these differ from the single mind, how could they not be the four views?
How may this be clarified? It is because taking emptiness and non-being as the Way is precisely "non-being. If it were "natural," [it would be different].
Whether it be the Great Ultimate (Tàijí) or the alternation of Yin and Yang as the Way (Dào), the Way is thus existence.
That there is both constant non-existence and constant existence means it is both non-existent and existent. That Yin and Yang are unfathomable means it is neither existent nor non-existent.

Some former scholars have said that that which wondrously transforms all things is called the Spirit (Shén); if it is not a thing, then it is also non-existent. Therefore, the great masters of the Western Heaven (India)...
All those who maintain that there are phenomena external to the mind are considered heterodox; that all phenomena are but mind alone is the orthodox teaching.

For when the mind is taken as the fundamental principle, all views naturally vanish. Although their words may differ, they are not sufficient to constitute a true difference. [To hold that] there are phenomena external to the mind...
Consequently, various views compete to arise; though their words may occasionally coincide, they are not yet sufficient to constitute true agreement.

Nevertheless, the sages of Confucianism and Daoism were certainly not unaware of this, but simply set it aside without discussion. This was primarily because they did not immediately and explicitly point toward the single mind (ekacitta).
It is the source of all dharmas; though it may be spoken of, it remains beyond discursive argument.

Just as the non-Buddhist practitioners of the Western Heavens are all Great Power Bodhisattvas manifesting through transformation, they display various activities that give rise to manifold views and exhaustively pursue heterodox paths in order to clarify that the Buddha-dharma is the true Way.
This is why it is called the Way of the Sage: both the conforming and the contrary take it as their source, yet it is not a matter of intellectual thought.
This is what can be understood through deliberation. Thus, there is an ancient saying: "In the past, before the True Doctrine had arrived, Confucius merely took it as a point of mental focus.
Now that we know where the ultimate principle resides, we ought not to continue clinging to provisional teachings.

However, to know that the provisional is provisional does not necessarily mean one knows the provisional; only when one knows that the provisional is the real does one truly know the provisional. This is also the way of the Duke of Zhou, Confucius, and Laozi.
The fundamental intent behind Master Zhuang’s establishment of teachings and formulation of words is the beginning and the end of the Great Matter (ekamahā-karaṇīya-dharmaparyāya).
Thus, the Three Teachings share a single mind; though they follow different paths, they travel the same road. As for the ultimate source of the Way, it is fundamentally beyond words and speech.
Were it not for the Mahāsattva Vimalakīrti, who else could understand this meaning?

The critique states: Qingliang did not judge Confucianism and Daoism to be heterodox; rather, he judged them by means of the Buddha-dharma and then attempted to harmonize them with Confucianism and Daoism.
Indeed, he failed to establish their fundamental tenets based on the nature of mind, instead merely pursuing their words and symbols.
To gauge its depth by its surface thunder is, as Mencius said, "not to measure the root but to level the tip.
One might make a mere square-inch piece of wood appear higher than a towering peak; how could this possibly be logical? This treatise is concise in expression yet exhaustive in meaning;
its scope is vast yet its boundaries are strict. Even one with an endless tongue three feet long would have no ground upon which to exercise their sophistry.
Truly so! He was indeed a master sage of our own age and a great Bodhisattva who protected the Teaching.
When National Teacher Wuye Dada of Fenzhou ascended the hall, a monk asked:

"The twelve divisions of the teachings have flowed into this land, and those who have attained the fruits of the Way are not merely one or two. Why did the Patriarch come to the East and separately proclaim the Mysterious Ultimate?"
"Directly pointing at the human mind, seeing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood"—how could it be that the World-Honored One’s preaching of the Dharma has any part that remains incomplete?

It is simply because the eminent monks of past generations all mastered the nine schools of thought and were profoundly enlightened in the Tripitaka; masters such as Daosheng, Sengzhao, Tanyue, and Daorong were all divine anomalies who appeared in the world.
How could they have been unaware of the depth and breadth of the Buddha-dharma? I, [Name], am ignorant and dull-witted; I pray that the Master will instruct me."
Shi said: "The Buddhas have never appeared in the world, nor have they bestowed a single dharma upon anyone.

It is only by administering remedies according to the illness that the twelve divisions of the teachings came into being—like exchanging honeyed fruit for bitter gourds, to wash away the karmic roots of you all."

There is not a single thing that possesses substantial reality. The supernatural transformations and the hundreds of thousands of gates of samādhi are all for the purpose of converting those celestial Māras and non-Buddhists.
The dual adornments of merit and wisdom are intended to shatter the views of clinging to existence and stagnating in emptiness.

If you do not comprehend the Way and the intent behind the Patriarchs' coming, what does it matter who they were—Sengzhao, Sengshao, Fayong, or Daorong? Today in this world, those who claim to understand Chan and the Way are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
They speak of the Buddha and speak of the mind, yet they possess hundreds of thousands of millions of afflictions; not even a speck of dust has been removed, and thus they have not escaped saṃsāra.

Their discursive thoughts do not cease, and they must all sink into the depths. Such as these cannot even recognize the fruits of their own karma, yet they falsely claim to benefit both themselves and others.

They call themselves those of the highest stream and place themselves on par with the former masters. They merely say that everything before one's eyes is nothing but the Buddha’s work, and that every step one takes...

All these are sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Yet, when one examines their habitual practices, they are not even equal to a single ordinary person who observes the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths of action.
When observing their speech, they disparage the bodhisattvas of the three vehicles and the ten stages. Now, the supreme flavor of clarified butter (*sarpis*) is a rarity in the world;
yet when encountered by such people, it turns instead into a poisonous drug. Even Nanshan did not permit this, calling them "those who merely parrot the words of the Mahāyāna."
They vie for supremacy amidst their lips and tongues, drumming up arguments on matters that have no form, competing with other former worthies; truly, how bitter it is!

Even a reclusive gentleman of the wilds understands to rest his head upon stones and rinse his mouth in mountain streams, renouncing profit and honor, yet he still possesses strategies for securing the state and governing the people, refusing to attend when summoned.
How much more so for us in the Zen school, whose path is distinct? Behold the ancients!

The virtuous person who follows the Way, after attaining the realization of its intent, dwells in thatched huts and stone chambers. For twenty or thirty years, they eat their meals from a broken-legged cauldron;
fame and profit do not touch their hearts, and wealth and treasure are not even considered. Having utterly forgotten the ways of the world, they conceal their traces among the mountain crags.
Though kings may summon them, they do not come; though feudal lords may invite them, they do not attend. How could they be compared to those like us who are greedy?
This is called "seeking profit through attachment. Immersed in the worldly path, one is like a petty peddler who has small desires but forgets the great fruit.
One might ask: "Do the worthies of the Ten Stages not understand the Buddha-principle? Could they not be like a single ordinary person of vast capacity? Truly, there is no such principle.
Though others preach the Dharma like clouds and rain, they were still rebuked by the Buddha, who said their realization of nature was as if separated by fine gauze. It is simply...
Out of concern for the standards of the sages and observing the present causes and effects, one is unable to transcend the sagely mind or go beyond all traces of the past.

The eminent worthies of antiquity, the great scholars and men of high virtue, who were profoundly learned in both ancient and modern times and possessed a penetrating understanding of the net of the teachings, generally used their knowledge and studies to interpret the texts;

thus, it was difficult to distinguish between water and milk, and they failed to clarify the self-nature. They merely contemplated stillness in pursuit of the Truth. Alas! Those who have obtained a human body are as rare as...
The soil upon one's fingernails is like those who have lost their human form; the soil of the great earth is like those who have attained it—how truly lamentable this is!

Even if there are those who awaken to the principle, possessing a single point of knowledge or understanding, they do not realize that this is the rule within awakening and the gateway for entering the principle.

They instead claim to have forever transcended worldly benefits, wandering through mountains and beside mountain streams while disregarding the superior current. Consequently, their mental outflows remain inexhaustible, and the principle...
If one's practice on the stages (*bhūmi*) is not clear, one will reach old age and death without achieving anything; it is merely a vain extension of years and months.

Furthermore, intelligence cannot oppose karma, and dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) does not exempt one from the wheel of suffering. Even if one’s talent were equal to Aśvaghoṣa and one’s understanding matched that of Nāgārjuna, such a person would only avoid losing their human form for one or two lifetimes.
If one’s faculties and thoughts have been purified in past lives, one will understand immediately upon hearing [the Dharma], as was the case with Master Sengzhao—what more could be required?

This is to be envied. You are far removed from the Way. When you and your brothers discuss reality and not the unreal, even these very mouthfuls of food and garments upon your bodies are entirely used to deceive the worthy and mislead the sages.
You seek them for the future, yet when observed by their hearts and their eyes of wisdom, they are like eating pus and blood;
you must repay them all before you can be free. Who possesses the fruit of the Way who could naturally inspire such trust?
Regarding those who give but do not receive: a bodhisattva training in Prajñāpāramitā must not deceive themselves. It is like walking upon the edge of an icicle or running upon the blade of a sword.

At the time of death, if even a single hair’s breadth of the conceptualizing mind of ordinary beings or sages is not exhausted, or if even a speck of dust of thought has not been forgotten, one will take birth according to that thought.
With the five aggregates—light or heavy—one will be conceived within the womb of a donkey or a horse, or fall into the hells.
Once they have been boiled thoroughly in the cauldron of boiling water, all their previous memorization, recollection, understanding, and wisdom are entirely lost at once.
They return once more to be ants, and from the beginning again become mosquitoes and gadflies; though these were indeed virtuous causes.
Yet they encounter evil fruits. What are you brothers striving for? It is solely because the nature of greed has bound you to the twenty-five states of existence beneath your very heels;

there will be no time of accomplishment. The Patriarch observed that the sentient beings of this land possess the root-nature of the Mahayana, so he transmitted only the Mind-Seal to point out their deluded state. Those who attain it do not distinguish between the ordinary and the holy.
O Sage! Between the foolish and the wise, it is better to have little reality than much emptiness. A true man of great character should, right now, simply come to rest;

suddenly stilling all conditions, he transcends the stream of birth and death and stands far beyond ordinary patterns. With his numinous light shining alone, he is not constrained by worldly entanglements.
Majestic and dignified, he walks alone through the three realms. Why must one be six feet tall with a complexion like purple-polished gold?
Radiant, with a circular halo upon the crown of the head and the mark of a broad and long tongue. To see me by means of form is to walk a deviant path.
Even if one possesses a retinue and adornments, they are obtained without seeking; mountains, rivers, and the great earth do not obstruct the eye-sight. One attains the Great Dhāraṇī.
Upon hearing it once, they attained awakening in a thousand ways, never seeking even the price of a single meal.
If you all were not like this, the arrival of the Patriarch in this land would have been neither beneficial nor detrimental. As for what is beneficial:

among hundreds or thousands of people, he might rescue one or two who are fit to be vessels of the Dharma. As for what is detrimental, it has already been clarified above: following others based on the Three [Teachings].

If one practices according to the teachings of the vehicles, it does not hinder the attainment of the four fruits and the three stages of worthiness; there is still a distinction between cultivation and progress.
Thus, the former masters said: "When realized, karmic obstacles are originally empty; when not yet realized, one must still repay past debts."
The critique states: The decline of the Chan school was already like this at that time; why, then, should we be surprised by later generations?

Thus, those with resolve may still distinguish between the raw and the matured, verify success and failure, weigh what to diminish and what to augment, and deliberate upon advancement and retreat, so as not to be swept away by the waves of the world.
Having lost its essential nature, this treatise is precisely the excellent medicine for curing the maladies of our own day.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: Furthermore, the nature of all phenomena is entirely empty and non-existent.

The causes and conditions for which you harbor anger are likewise false and deceptive, as they lack any substantial reality; yet you undergo great suffering. It is like a Buddhist shrine located within a mountain.
Within that [monastery] there was a separate room. A ghost resided in the room and came to frighten and harass the practitioners;
therefore, all the practitioners abandoned the room and departed. A visiting monk arrived, and the *karmadāna* assigned him to stay in this room, saying to him:
"In this room there is a spirit who delights in harassing people. If you are able to dwell within it, then stay. The visiting monk, relying on his own [resolve], remained.
"Because of the power of my precepts and my great learning, what can this little demon do? I am able to subdue it. He then entered the room and stayed there.
In the evening, another monk came seeking a place to stay. The *karmadāna* also assigned him to stay in this same room and told him that a ghost was harassing people there.
That man also said, "What can this little demon do? I shall subdue it. The one who had entered first closed the door.

He sat upright, waiting for the ghost. A later arrival came at night in the darkness, knocking on the door seeking entry. The one who had entered first, thinking it was a ghost, did not open the door.
The later arrival knocked with all his might. The practitioner inside resisted with force, but the one outside prevailed; he pushed the door open and entered.
The one inside struck him, and the one outside also struck back with great force until dawn.

When they met in the morning, they were found to be old classmates; each felt ashamed and apologized to the other. The crowd gathered like clouds, laughing and finding it strange. Sentient beings are also like this:
within the five aggregates there is no person and no self, yet they vainly grasp at signs, leading to strife and contention.
Even if one’s body were dismembered and lying on the ground, there would be only bone and flesh, with neither person nor self. For this reason, the Bodhisattva says to sentient beings: "You..."
Do not engage in strife or commit offenses within the emptiness of the fundamental nature. Because of such strife, one may not even obtain a human body, let alone encounter a Buddha.
[The commentary] states:
The three poisons of sentient beings manifest in daily life; their faults are extremely grave, yet among them, the fault of the poison of anger is the most severe.

The loss is particularly grave. This is because one fails to realize that the external objects before them are fundamentally empty, and thus gives rise to false dualistic opposition within one's own mind.
Because of this dualism, the wind of anger and resentment is stirred up, which blows upon the fire of the mental consciousness, mutually incinerating the roots of goodness of both self and others.
Viewed with the correct eye, it is exactly like two bhikṣus who close a door and push against it, striking with all their might.
When a practitioner of the Way encounters adversity striking the mind and the arousal of anger erupts, if they can enter this contemplation, they will immediately feel a sense of release;
it will melt away like ice and crumble like a fortress. It is just like two bhikṣus meeting at dawn—they will naturally clap their hands and laugh together.
The Great Being Shanhui of the Liang Dynasty composed the *Verses on the Four Marks*. Regarding birth, he said: "Consciousness rests upon the rising bubble; birth comes from craving and desire.
In former times one was full-grown; today one is again an infant. Star-like eyes follow others' gazes; crimson lips open toward the breast."

Out of pity for those who are deluded regarding the nature of awakening, they instead spend kalpas undergoing the cycle of saṃsāra. Old Age said: "Beholding my reflection, my countenance has changed; ascending the steps, my vigor has withered. Alas!
Now that I am old, even my bowing and prostrations have become deficient. My body is like a tree on a precipice; my mind is like a turtle longing for water.
Yet I still indulge in outflows (āsrava) and refuse to study the Unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). Sickness said: "Suddenly I was struck by a deep-seated malady..."
One becomes a bedridden patient; wife and children grieve in silence; friends weary of one's presence. Piercing pain draws through a thousand vessels; moans reach the four neighbors.
Unaware of the perils of the path ahead, one still indulges in greed and anger at will. At death, it is said: "The vital spirit follows the path of birth;
the wandering soul enters the barrier of death. One hears only of millions departing, yet sees not a single person returning. The precious horse neighs in vain.
Standing, the courtyard flowers shall forever cease to be plucked. Having early sought the Unsurpassed Way, one should be spared from the mountains of the four directions.
[The commentary] says: Birth, old age, sickness, and death—these four most momentous matters converge upon a single body.

Viewed in this way, the entire substance of the ignorance manifesting in the daily activities of sentient beings is itself the four wisdoms of the enlightenment of all Buddhas. What consciousness, then, remains to be transformed? For consciousness is fundamentally...

As for the provisional vehicle’s teaching on the transformation of the five, eight, six, and seven consciousnesses from cause to fruit, this merely concerns the transformation of their conventional designations as they proceed from cause to fruit;

how could it be the innate, teacherless, spontaneous true wisdom inherent in humans? Only because there is no consciousness to be transformed can it be called true wisdom.
For consciousness (*vijñāna*) and wisdom (*jñāna*) are non-dual, being of one and the same nature. It is like water that freezes to become ice when cold, and melts to become water again when warm;

The Inscription on the Cessation of Mind by the Monk Wangming: Within the Dharma-realm there is a person who is like a wish-fulfilling jewel.
He seals his body with nine layers of restraint and inscribes upon his breast: "He was a man of the ancients who gathered his mind. Be cautious! Be cautious! Do not harbor excessive deliberations;

do not seek excessive knowledge. Excessive knowledge brings excessive affairs; it is better to let the will rest. Excessive deliberation brings excessive loss; it is better to maintain the One. When deliberations are many, the resolve falters."

Scatter it. Know that when the mind is distracted, distraction gives rise to affliction; when the will is scattered, it obstructs the Way. Do not say, "What harm is there? for its suffering is long-lasting.
Do not say, "What need is there to fear? for its calamities boil like a cauldron. If not a single drop of water is stopped, the four seas will soon be full;

if not a single speck of dust is brushed away, the Five Peaks will eventually be formed. To guard the end, one must attend to the root; though small, do not treat it lightly. It governs your seven apertures and closes off your six [senses].

Regarding emotions: do not seek them in form; do not listen for them in sound. He who hears sounds becomes deaf; he who sees forms becomes blind. A single literary work or a single art is like a gnat in the sky;
a single skill or a single talent is like a solitary lamp beneath the sun. To prize such refined talents and arts is to be obscured by folly.
One abandons simple purity and sinks into licentious beauty. It is easy to perceive when a horse bolts, but the mind-monkey is difficult to restrain. When the spirit is thus exhausted...

In service, one’s form will inevitably be worn away and exhausted; in perverse conduct, one is ultimately deluded, forever mired on the long journey. One does not value talent and ability, yet day by day grows ever more ignorant and dull-witted.
Boasting of one's own clumsiness while envying the skillful, one’s virtue is not expansive. When fame is thick but conduct is thin, its speed is such that it will swiftly collapse.

Internally harboring arrogance and self-praise, one externally incurs resentment and hatred. Whether spoken from the mouth or written by the hand, one seeks the reputation of others—this is truly a great peril.

What the vulgar call auspicious, the sages call a calamity. Pleasure and play are but momentary; sorrow and grief endure for long. To fear one’s shadow and fear one’s footprints is to go further and further away from the goal.
Sit upright in the shade of a tree, and the footprints vanish as the shadow sinks. Loathing birth and fearing old age, one creates karma with every thought.
If the workings of the mind are extinguished, the cycle of birth and death is forever severed. Neither dying nor being born, without form and without name—this is the single path of emptiness.
Quiescence. All things are equal and level; what is noble and what is base? What is disgraceful and what is honorable? What is superior and what is inferior? What is heavy and what is light?

Wuxing Yiming was a man of learning and integrity. When the Liang dynasty fell, he likely abandoned his official rank and clan name to enter the monastic life, adopting the name Wuming (Nameless).
Later, during the Western Zhou, the court sought to subvert his resolve, ordering high-ranking officials to entice him with prestigious posts.

Wuming personally recounted how his ancestral state had been overturned and presented seven reasons why returning to secular life was impossible. His oath was so poignant that they ultimately could not prevail against him. He further composed the "Poem on the Five Sufferings."
The meaning of this poem is lofty and pure; it was widely copied and circulated at the time.
Observing the "Inscription on the Cessation of Mind," it seems to have been composed during his later years, perhaps as a reflection upon his youthful preoccupation with literary composition.
